sections.title: Unit Vocabulary — Write each term in your own words
Lesson 1 — Lab Safety: The NFPA 704 Hazard Diamond
sections.objective: Read the four sections of the NFPA hazard diamond and explain what each rating means.
concept: Before you touch any chemical, read its hazard information. The NFPA 704 hazard diamond — sometimes called a 'fire diamond' — summarizes the major hazards of a chemical in one symbol. It has four colored sections: the top (red) diamond specifies the level of fire hazard, based on the flash point temperature. The blue (left) diamond indicates the health hazard. The yellow (right) diamond describes reactivity — how readily the substance will detonate or undergo violent chemical change. The white (bottom) diamond points out special hazards, such as oxidizers or substances that react with water.

Each hazard is rated from 0 to 4: 0 means no hazard, 4 means extremely hazardous. A chemical rated 4 for health is deadly even with brief exposure; a rating of 1 means mild irritation. Reading these numbers tells you how careful you need to be.

example.title: Worked Example — Reading a Hazard Diamond
example.problem: A container shows a hazard diamond rated 2-3-1 with a W in the white section. What do the ratings tell you?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Fire hazard (top, red) = 2: the substance must be moderately heated before it will ignite.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Health hazard (left, blue) = 3: even short exposure can cause serious injury or permanent damage.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Reactivity (right, yellow) = 1: stable normally, but can become unstable under high heat or pressure.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.text: Special (bottom, white) = W: the substance reacts violently with water.

example.answer: Handle with full PPE, away from water and flames.

sections.title: Lesson 2 — Physical vs Chemical Properties
sections.objective: Classify properties and changes of matter as physical or chemical.
concept: A physical property is a characteristic observed without changing the chemical composition — density, color, hardness, melting point, and boiling point are physical properties. A physical change alters the state or form but not the identity: wax melting, sugar dissolving, steam condensing, and grinding solids are physical changes.

A chemical property describes the ability of a substance to change into different matter — flammability, toxicity, acidity, and reactivity are chemical properties. Iron rusts (combines with oxygen); nitroglycerin explodes easily; neon is very unreactive. A chemical change always produces new substances: rusting, burning, food rotting, copper reacting with nitric acid.

example.title: Worked Example — Classifying Properties
example.problem: Classify each as a physical or chemical property: (a) the melting point of iron is 1538 °C; (b) chromium does not oxidize; (c) the density of aluminum is 2.70 g/cm³.

steps.label: Step 1
steps.text: Melting point is observed without changing the chemical composition — physical property.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.text: Resistance to oxidation describes how the substance behaves in a chemical reaction — chemical property.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.text: Density describes the substance itself, not a reaction — physical property.

practice.q: Classify: 'Iron combines with oxygen to form rust.'
Which is a PHYSICAL change?
Which is a CHEMICAL change?
Why is flammability a chemical property?
practice.answer: Burning changes the substance into new products (CO₂ and water) — a chemical change, so flammability is a chemical property.

sections.title: Lesson 3 — Measurements and SI Units
sections.objective: Identify SI base units, metric prefixes, and the three parts of every measurement.
concept: Every measurement provides three kinds of information: a number (magnitude), a unit (standard of comparison), and an indication of uncertainty. The SI system uses base units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), and kelvin (temperature).

Metric prefixes change the size of a unit by powers of ten. Common prefixes: kilo (k, 1000×), centi (c, 1/100), milli (m, 1/1000), micro (µ, 1/1,000,000), nano (n, 1/1,000,000,000). Derived units include volume (liter = dm³) and density (g/mL or g/cm³).

sections.title: Lesson 4 — Significant Figures
sections.objective: Count significant figures and report calculations with the correct number of sig figs.
concept: Significant figures (sig figs) are the digits in a measurement that are known with certainty plus one estimated digit. Rules: non-zero digits are always significant; leading zeros are NOT significant (0.003080 has 4 sig figs — the 3080); captive zeros between non-zeros ARE significant; trailing zeros are significant only if a decimal point is present.

Calculations: for multiplication and division, round the answer to the fewest significant figures of any factor. For addition and subtraction, round to the fewest decimal places. Exact numbers (counted or defined) have unlimited sig figs.

sections.title: Lesson 5 — Dimensional Analysis and Density
sections.objective: Convert units using conversion factors and calculate density.
concept: Dimensional analysis (unit conversion) uses conversion factors written as ratios to cancel unwanted units. Example: 12.0 oz × (29.57 mL / 1 oz) = 355 mL — the oz units cancel, leaving mL.
Density is the ratio of mass to volume: density = mass / volume. The density of aluminum is 2.70 g/cm³ — a small piece and a large block have the same density (it is intensive).
